title: REST API Development Quick Reference
description: Look up a lesson idea, see its small example, and check a common mistake. Open the linked lesson for setup and practice steps.

entries.name: Name a resource
entries.summary: A resource is a thing an API exposes. /books/1 names one book, while /books names a collection.

example.code:
GET /books/1 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.test

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":1,"title":"Moon Trip"}

notes: Use resource names clearly; a URL should identify what is being addressed.

entries.name: Read without changing data
entries.summary: GET asks to read a resource. Reading this collection does not add or remove books.

example.code:
GET /books HTTP/1.1
Host: example.test

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

[{"id":1,"title":"Moon Trip"}]

notes: Do not design a GET route that deletes a record.

entries.name: Create a resource
entries.summary: POST sends data for the collection to handle. A successful creation often returns 201 and a Location header.

example.code:
POST /books HTTP/1.1
Host: example.test
Content-Type: application/json

{"title":"Sun Trip"}

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /books/2
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":2,"title":"Sun Trip"}

notes: A repeated POST can create another item unless the API provides a duplicate-prevention rule.

entries.name: Replace a known resource
entries.summary: PUT supplies the desired representation at a known URL. This example replaces the book title and page count.

example.code:
PUT /books/1 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.test
Content-Type: application/json

{"title":"Moon Trip","pages":30}

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":1,"title":"Moon Trip","pages":30}

notes: Know whether the API treats omitted fields as removed when using PUT.

entries.name: Change part of a resource
entries.summary: PATCH can send only changes. This example uses JSON Merge Patch to change the page count.

example.code:
PATCH /books/1 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.test
Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json

{"pages":30}

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":1,"title":"Moon Trip","pages":30}

notes: PATCH formats have different rules; name the media type you support.

entries.name: Remove a resource
entries.summary: DELETE asks to remove the target resource. A 204 success response has no body.

example.code:
DELETE /books/1 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.test

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content

notes: Do not attach a JSON body to a 204 response.

entries.name: Report an unknown item
entries.summary: 404 means the requested resource was not found. A short error body can help a client explain the problem.

example.code:
GET /books/99 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.test

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/json

{"error":"Book not found"}

notes: Do not return 200 for every outcome; clients use status codes.

entries.name: Choose matching results
entries.summary: A query string can describe a filter. The exact parameter names belong to the API design.

example.code:
GET /books?colour=blue HTTP/1.1
Host: example.test

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

[{"id":1,"colour":"blue"}]

notes: Document filter rules rather than making clients guess them.

entries.name: Read a small page of results
entries.summary: Pagination divides a large collection into smaller pieces. This example returns a next link.

example.code:
GET /books?limit=1 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.test

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"items":[{"id":1}],"next":"/books?after=1&limit=1"}

notes: Use a stable ordering so items do not jump between pages.

entries.name: Describe the body format
entries.summary: Content-Type says what format a body uses. Accept says which response formats the client can understand.

example.code:
GET /books/1 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.test
Accept: application/json

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":1}

notes: JSON text needs valid quoting; a header alone does not make invalid text valid JSON.

entries.name: Repeat a request safely
entries.summary: An idempotent operation has the same intended final effect when repeated. Setting pages to 30 twice leaves it at 30.
notes: Same final effect does not require every repeated response to have the same status.

entries.name: Reuse an unchanged response
entries.summary: An ETag labels a version. If-None-Match asks whether that version is still current. A 304 has no new body.

example.code:
GET /books/1 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.test
If-None-Match: "book-v1"

HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified
ETag: "book-v1"

notes: A client needs a cached body to reuse; 304 does not contain the resource data.
